conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure you’re getting the emotional support you deserve now that your little one has arrived.

Today I’ll be using a short, widely trusted questionnaire called the EPDS—short for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand how you’re coping so we can be sure you have whatever help you might need.

Everything you share is confidential and stays between us unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger. We’ll keep the conversation relaxed and unrushed, and we can pause any time.

Ready to begin? I’ll ask the questions conversationally—no checkboxes needed. Let’s start:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve still been able to laugh a little—like if I see a funny reel or my partner does something silly—but it definitely doesn’t come as easily as before the baby. Sometimes I’ll start to smile and then it just fades, like I’m too tired or distracted to really enjoy the moment.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like if my partner makes a goofy face or we watch a funny clip—but it feels kind of forced, you know? I’ll catch myself smiling, but it fades fast. I guess I’m just too tired or preoccupied to really enjoy it the way I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some stuff—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes to hold the baby so I can take a shower—but the excitement is pretty mild. Mostly I’m just thinking about what needs to get done next instead of actually enjoying the moment.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding her right or I missed her sleepy window.” It’s silly because I know babies cry, but the thought still pops up that I’m falling short somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A couple of nights this week I woke up in a bit of a panic—just suddenly sure something was wrong with the baby, even though she was breathing fine in her bassinet. It only lasted a few minutes and I could calm myself, but it felt weird to be on edge without any real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, that happened once or twice. Out of nowhere my heart started racing and I got this wave of “what if something bad happens?”—like I had to jump up and check on her even though she was sleeping peacefully. It passed pretty quickly, maybe five minutes, but it left me jittery for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When she’s fussy and the laundry’s piled up and I can’t even get a shower in, it feels like I’m drowning a little. I usually manage—my partner steps in or I hand her off to Grandma—but those stretches where everything hits at once leave me pretty frazzled.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’m tired enough that once my head hits the pillow I’m usually out. Every few nights my mind will race—mostly running through feeding times or wondering if she’s breathing—but I still drift off within twenty minutes or so.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had moments—like when she won’t latch or I’m just sitting alone feeding at three a.m.—where a wave of sadness hits. It’s not all day, but maybe once a day I’ll tear up and feel kind of heavy before I shake it off.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, that happened twice this week—nothing huge set it off. Once was when she wouldn’t nap and I just sat on the couch with tears rolling down while I rocked her. The other time was after a call from my mother-in-law; she meant well, but I still ended up crying in the bathroom for a couple of minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed or teary, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

You've shared how the last week has felt heavy: laughter comes out forced and fades quickly, excitement is mild and task-focused, and waves of sadness or tears arrive most days. You described sudden nighttime panic that sends you checking the baby even when all is well, and moments when chores and crying jags leave you feeling “drowning.” At the same time you can still enjoy small comforts, you sleep when the baby sleeps, and you have never thought of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing only sometimes and describing it as forced and quickly fading aligns with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only mild enjoyment and persistent distraction by tasks, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a few times" in the past week, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes waking in panic about baby's safety without cause, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response describes discrete panic episodes occurring "once or twice," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 15 places you above the 14-point threshold indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. Core symptoms aligning with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> include: diminished interest/pleasure (<quote>laughter feels forced and fades</quote>), depressed mood most days (<quote>wave of sadness hits once a day</quote>), excessive guilt (<quote>I must be doing something wrong</quote>), and associated anxiety/panic episodes. <sym>Sleep disruption</sym> is minimal and <sym>self-harm ideation</sym> is absent, ruling out immediate safety risk but still warranting prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss score and mood
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or therapist trained in CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression
3. Begin daily mood/sleep tracking to share at your visit
4. Maximize rest: accept help with night feeds, nap when baby naps, keep fluids/snacks bedside
5. Spend 10-15 min outdoors or doing gentle movement; light exposure can lift mood
6. Share these results with a trusted support person so they can help monitor changes
7. Seek immediate care (call 911 or go to ER) if thoughts of self-harm or harm to baby ever arise
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, approx. 2–3 wks post-delivery (per chart)  
Date: ___

1. Positive indicators for mood screening  
   - Anhedonia: reports laughter “forced/fleeting,” limited anticipatory enjoyment  
   - Daily sadness/tearfulness: 1–2×/week spontaneous crying, “heaviness” most days  
   - Excessive guilt: attributes infant fussing to personal failure (“must be doing something wrong”)  
   - Overwhelm: “feels like drowning” when tasks accumulate, needs support to cope  
   - Anxiety: multiple nocturnal panic episodes (<5 min) with urge to check sleeping infant, persistent worry  
   - Sleep: generally sleeps when infant sleeps; occasional racing thoughts but no frank insomnia

2. Absent / negative indicators  
   - No self-harm ideation (endorsed “never”)  
   - No persistent insomnia or appetite changes reported  
   - No loss of attachment to infant

3. Pattern summary  
   Mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms with concurrent anxiety, congruent with possible postpartum depression/anxiety, not meeting severity for urgent safety concerns.

4. Risk factors noted  
   - Daily low mood with crying spells  
   - Diminished pleasure/joy  
   - Unwarranted self-blame  
   - Episodic panic-like symptoms  
   - Perceived role overload

5. Screening recommendation  
   Score suggests further evaluation with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) or similar validated tool; consider referral for counseling and/or medical follow-up to rule out postpartum depression/anxiety disorder. No immediate safety issues identified.
